nodes.text: Researchers who want to build agents that act on the world through real software (code, shell, browser) must assemble the interaction interface, the safe execution environment, a tool library, multi-agent support, and evaluation from separate, incompatible frameworks.
nodes.audience_note: Reader needs to know: an LLM agent takes actions in an environment and receives observations back (N33).

nodes.text: Software is already humans' most general, powerful interface for acting on the world, so giving agents robust software interaction is a direct route to broadly useful, real-world-capable agents.

Prior open frameworks each supply useful pieces: general orchestration with basic runtime support (LangChain/LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI), one capability done well (BrowserGym for browsing, DSPy for prompt optimization), multi-agent orchestration patterns (MetaGPT, GPTSwarm), or GitHub-issue-fixing specialization (SWE-Agent, AutoCodeRover, ChatDev, AgentCoder).

None of these combines a general (not domain-specific) sandboxed code-and-browser runtime, a standardized/extensible tool library, multi-agent delegation, and an integrated evaluation harness in one open platform; and no prior generalist agent had been evaluated this broadly, unmodified, against category specialists.
RQ1: Can one open platform supply, together, the interaction mechanism, safe execution, extensible tooling, multi-agent support, and evaluation that existing frameworks provide only piecemeal?
RQ2: Once built, can a single generalist agent running on that platform -- with no per-benchmark modification -- perform competitively across qualitatively different task categories?

H: one unmodified CodeActAgent will reach performance comparable to, though not necessarily exceeding, category-specialist and prior domain-general baselines in all three categories. A result far below baselines in most benchmarks of two or more categories would count against H.

Build an open platform with these five pieces, and evaluate one generalist agent built on it across 15 established benchmarks spanning software engineering, web browsing, and other assistance tasks, without benchmark-specific prompt engineering.

OpenHands: an event-stream architecture connects an agent to a Docker-sandboxed runtime (bash shell, IPython, and a Playwright browser) through three core actions, an AgentSkills tool library bounded by an explicit inclusion rule, an AgentDelegateAction for multi-agent delegation, an AgentHub of implemented agents, and mocked-LLM integration tests for regression QC.

Evaluation protocol: one CodeActAgent (delegating browser sub-tasks to BrowsingAgent; a GPTSwarm-orchestrated variant for GAIA) is run zero-shot, without benchmark-specific prompt changes, on 15 benchmarks across three categories, and compared against each benchmark's own published baselines.
Software-engineering results: SWE-Bench Lite resolve rate and HumanEvalFix pass rate for OpenHands vs. published baselines.
Web-browsing results: WebArena success rate (competitive with the prior domain-general baseline, below trained specialists) and MiniWoB++ success rate (well below a trained RL specialist).

Miscellaneous-assistance results: GAIA, GPQA, AgentBench (OS subset), MINT (math/code), ProofWriter, and Entity Deduction Arena success rates for OpenHands vs. published baselines and, where available, humans.

Taken together, the same unmodified CodeActAgent is competitive across all three categories on most of the 15 benchmarks, which the authors contrast with baseline agents that are typically built and tuned for one category.

Within the same agent scaffold, score scales strongly with backbone-LLM capability (e.g. MINT math/code, AgentBench-OS, SWE-Bench Lite), suggesting the residual gap to specialists tracks the backbone model at least as much as it tracks the platform's architecture; an architecture-driven, category-specific explanation is considered and judged less likely because the prompt is unmodified across categories.

The platform closes the capability gap by construction: each of the five pieces that prior frameworks split across projects is present and demonstrated (via the 15-benchmark run) in one open codebase.
An open, MIT-licensed platform (OpenHands) that combines a general sandboxed code-and-browser runtime, an extensible tool library, multi-agent delegation, and an integrated evaluation harness.
Empirical demonstration that a single generalist agent, without per-category modification, is competitive across software-engineering, web-browsing, and miscellaneous-assistance benchmarks.
Author-stated (L001): multi-modal file handling (images, video, office documents) is not yet integrated in a principled way through standard IPython/browser channels.
Author-stated (L002), broad: current agents (including OpenHands') still struggle with complex tasks.
Author-stated (L003): the current agent performs poorly when editing long files.
Author-stated (L004): the HumanEvalFix comparison against SWE-Agent's 87.7% is not matched (1-shot demonstration vs. OpenHands' 0-shot).
Author-stated (L005): OpenHands' own agent workflows still require substantial handcrafted engineering.

Writer-derived (L006): baselines differ in backbone LLM, shot count, and training regime (prompted vs. fine-tuned vs. RL-trained specialist), so this is not a controlled, single-variable ablation of the architecture alone.
Writer-derived (L007): every benchmark cell is a single run, with no reported seed/trial variance.
Writer-derived (L008): the competitiveness pattern is not universal -- MiniWoB++ and the MINT code subset are counterexamples where OpenHands clearly trails a baseline/specialist.

Generality can come from a sufficiently general interaction interface plus a shared runtime, rather than from bespoke per-task scaffolding; most of the remaining gap to specialists is better explained by backbone-model capability than by task category.
Open, extensible infrastructure lowers the barrier to agent research and can accelerate community-driven progress, consistent with the project's continued growth and expansion after publication.
Building stronger agents through both training-time and inference-time techniques.
Automatic workflow generation via graph-based frameworks, reducing today's handcrafted workflow construction.
Principled multi-modality support through standard IPython/browser integration with vision-language models.
Integrating an optional retry/self-correction component (Reflexion-style prompts plus a completion reward model) into the browsing agent.
An LLM agent perceives environment state and produces an action; the action is executed and returns an observation, which becomes part of the next state -- an action/observation loop.

nodes.text: Sandboxed execution: agent-written code and commands run inside an isolated container, not on the host machine, so a mistake or malicious output cannot damage the user's own system.
nodes.audience_note: Needed before describing the Docker runtime.

nodes.text: Benchmark success metrics used below are simple pass/resolve rates or accuracies (percentage of task instances solved), not loss or perplexity; higher is better throughout.

Agent-Computer Interface (ACI): the specific set of tools/commands exposed to an agent for acting on its environment; a better-designed ACI can change how well the same underlying LLM performs, independent of the LLM itself.

experiment_chains.hypothesis: One unmodified CodeActAgent will resolve/fix issues at a rate comparable to specialist SWE agents.
experiment_chains.falsifier: A resolve/pass rate far below every specialist baseline would count against the hypothesis.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: SWE-Bench Lite is used instead of the full set for cost, and without hint text, to keep the setting realistic (E031); HumanEvalFix reuses the benchmark's own pass@k protocol for comparability (E098-adjacent).
experiment_chains.next: Establishes competitiveness in one category; the next question is whether the same agent transfers to a qualitatively different interaction style (open-ended web browsing).

experiment_chains.hypothesis: The same generalist agent, now acting through a browser instead of a shell, will still be comparable to a prior domain-general baseline.
experiment_chains.falsifier: A success rate far below the prior domain-general baseline (WebArena Agent) on both benchmarks would count against the hypothesis.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: BrowsingAgent reuses WebArena's own observation/action style so the comparison is to a like-for-like domain-general baseline (E018).
experiment_chains.next: Competitiveness holds against the domain-general baseline but not against trained specialists (MiniWoB++); the next question is whether this pattern -- solid against general baselines, more mixed against specialists -- also holds in categories further from code and browsing altogether.

experiment_chains.experiment: GAIA, GPQA, AgentBench, MINT, ProofWriter, Entity Deduction Arena (miscellaneous assistance)
experiment_chains.hypothesis: The same agent, unmodified again, will remain comparable to each benchmark's own baseline across a further six benchmarks that share neither code-editing nor browsing as their primary skill.
experiment_chains.falsifier: A success rate far below the benchmark's own baseline agent on most of these six benchmarks would count against the hypothesis.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: Benchmark-native baselines and, for GPQA, human performance bands are used as reference points because they are what each benchmark's own paper reports (E091, E093, E095, E098, E100, E102).
experiment_chains.next: Having tested all three categories, the results are synthesized into one cross-category interpretation (N14) and checked against the one exception pattern (MiniWoB++/MINT-code) before drawing implications.
